analysis.one_liner: Lets state, local, and tribal governments run public banks with no-fee accounts, 15% interest caps, and postal banking.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to four House committees the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let states, cities, tribes, and local governments own banks that operate for the public instead of for shareholders. These public banks would offer accounts with no fees, minimum balances, or overdraft charges, cap the interest they charge borrowers at 15%, and work with post offices so people could bank at their local branch. The Federal Reserve would provide them with payment services, liquidity, and grants, and the FDIC would insure their deposits without the usual dollar limit. The bill never moved: it was referred to four committees on the day it was introduced and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People without bank accounts or stuck with costly ones: roughly 4.5% of U.S. households are unbanked, and many more pay overdraft and minimum-balance fees. Public bank accounts would carry no fees and no overdraft charges, and public bank loans could not charge more than 15% interest. Low-income communities, environmental justice communities, and tribes would get dedicated representation on bank boards and targeted lending. State and local governments would earn higher interest on the money they already hold, and rural and low-income areas would gain banking access through post offices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unbanked and underbanked households; low-income communities

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets the Federal Reserve charter public banks wholly owned by state, tribal, or local governments, or recognize existing ones.
Public bank accounts for individuals could not charge fees, require minimum balances, or impose overdraft fees or penalties.
Interest on any retail loan from a public bank could not exceed 15% a year, including all finance charges, with penalties for charging more.
The FDIC must insure deposits at public banks without regard to the total deposit amount, beyond the standard $250,000 limit that applies to ordinary banks.
The Postal Service must partner with public banks to offer account and payment services at post offices, funded by the Federal Reserve.
Public banks would get Federal Reserve services including payment accounts, digital dollar accounts (FedAccounts), liquidity facilities, and access to a grant program for startup costs.
Public bank boards must include community, labor, environmental, and marginalized-group representatives, and banks cannot finance fossil fuel production or infrastructure.
Loans of $500,000 or more must pay Davis-Bacon prevailing wages, and borrowers may not oppose unionization on projects using public funds.

analysis.who_pays: Private commercial banks would face a publicly backed competitor offering free accounts and 15% interest ceilings, and could lose deposits, especially from state and local governments. Payday and other high-cost lenders would be undercut where public banks lend. Fossil fuel companies, gun manufacturers, private prisons, and tobacco companies would be barred from public bank financing. The cost of unlimited deposit insurance and Fed services would ultimately sit on the public side of the ledger, and the bill records those expenses so they do not reduce the Fed's payments to the Treasury.
analysis.who_pays_short: Commercial banks, payday lenders, fossil fuel firms

drawbacks.text: Unlimited deposit insurance removes the $250,000 cap that protects the FDIC fund, and the bill directs the FDIC to use an 'alternative risk profile' that favors public banks, shifting more potential loss onto the insurance fund that private banks pay into.

The Federal Reserve must pay public banks above-market interest on government deposits (at least the overnight target rate plus 2%) and cover all operating costs, with the expenses recorded so they do not reduce the Fed's remittances to the Treasury — meaning the costs land on the public rather than showing up in a budget line.
Existing public banks, such as the state-owned Bank of North Dakota, would be exempt from most of the bill's consumer, labor, and governance rules unless they take a startup grant.

Public banks would be prohibited from financing fossil fuel projects, gun manufacturers, private prisons, tobacco companies, and firms with history of tax avoidance or CEO pay above 100-to-1, which supporters see as screening and critics see as politically directed lending.

Banks run by governments raise a fair concern about lending decisions being steered by elected officials rather than credit standards; the bill's response is community representation on boards and public annual reports, which limits but does not eliminate that risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people the bill targets — the unbanked, fee-paying account holders, and borrowers facing triple-digit-interest loans — the benefits are direct and concrete: free accounts, a 15% rate ceiling, and banking at post offices. The serious costs are financial-system ones: unlimited deposit insurance and above-market interest paid by the Fed are real obligations, and the bill's choice to record them as 'deferred assets' outside the Fed's balance sheet makes the true cost harder to see. Community banks and credit unions would face new competition, though the bill offers them coordination grants. On balance the design favors account holders and borrowers over financial-sector incumbents, with the honest caveat that the public backstops are large and loosely costed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, sent to one subcommittee two days later, and no committee ever held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the Public Banking Act of 2023 on December 13, 2023, joined as an original cosponsor by Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Pressley, Lee of California, Schakowsky, and Omar.
The bill was referred the same day to the Financial Services Committee and additionally to Oversight, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce.
Two days later it was referred to the Energy, Climate and Grid Security Subcommittee — the last action ever recorded.
Seven Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial banks, payday and other high-cost lenders, and fossil fuel companies are better off because the bill died: no publicly owned competitor with fee-free accounts and a 15% rate cap ever got created, and the banking status quo — including overdraft fees and high-cost credit — continues unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led Financial Services Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: A government-owned network offering no-fee accounts, 15% rate caps, unlimited insurance, and post-office access would compete directly for deposits and borrowers, and the bill requires public banks to pay governments above-market interest on their deposits. Banks currently profit from overdraft fees and high card rates that the public alternative would undercut.
Public bank credit capped at 15% APR would offer a far cheaper alternative wherever these banks lend. These lenders' business model depends on rates far above that cap.
Public banks are prohibited from financing fossil fuel production, processing, or infrastructure in any form, foreclosing a potential public funding source.

industries.industry: Gun makers, private prisons, and tobacco companies
industries.note: Public banks could not provide loans, investments, or financial services to companies in these industries, cutting them off from any new public financing channel.

industries.industry: Community development financial institutions and credit unions
industries.note: The bill makes state and local entities eligible as CDFIs and creates grants for coordination between public banks, CDFIs, minority deposit institutions, and credit unions. They gain partners and funding rather than a direct competitor in the bill's design.
